newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Czarnikow chief sees Australia on top in sugar.
newsitem.headline: Czarnikow chief sees Australia on top in sugar.

text.p: The Australian sugar industry would be more capable than its international competitors of taking advantage of emerging opportunities for growth when sugar prices began to gain in 1998 and 1999, John Barneby, managing director of C. Czarnikow Sugar Ltd, said on Tuesday.

Addressing the CANEGROWERS annual meeting here, Barneby spoke glowingly of the relative strength and performance of Australia's main sugar state, Queensland, compared with other leading sugar producers.

"It is ... likely that the world (sugar) price will remain under pressure this year but if 10 cents (U.S. a pound) proves to be the low point for this cycle, then you will be more capable than any other industry to take advantage of emerging opportunities for growth when prices begin to lift again in 1998 and 1999," he told the meeting of Queensland canegrowers.
Difficult adjustments remained to be made in many of the largest sugar producers in the world, he said.
"Australia, by contrast, has a well-developed industry with a high degree of mechanisation and efficiency," he said.
"There are economies of scale throughout the system and dedicated export terminals that can turn around large vessels in the shortest time," Barneby said.
Competitors' costs were on an upward path and provided Australian sugar remained competitive, consumers would prefer to buy from a producer with Australia's superior service, he said.
He predicted Australian sugar would show continuing expansion in the quantity and destination of exports.
Discussing Australia's competition, Barneby said Brazil had overtaken India to this season produce the world's largest cane harvest of almost 285 million tonnes.
But behind the success were serious problems. Exports were not tailored to customers needs but were mainly surplus from crystal sugar produced for the domestic market, he said.
Rapid growth and an income stream which needed consolidating meant it would not be surprising if more Brazilian sugar mill bankruptcies emerged over the next few years, he said.
Infrastructure was also stretched, he said.
In India, rigid government management left the industry liable to large and regular swings in its sugar balance.
"Because of its scale (this) will be a major regional and world market influence," he said. "Even when deregulation is tackled, there will be a period of adjustment and potential instability."

Thailand, Australia's main regional competitor, was low-cost and highly responsive to the marketplace but decisions needed to be taken about infrastructure investment and mechanising field operations, he said.
Without these, recent growth may level off while, if the investment is undertaken, Thailand may find it difficult to present itself as a low-cost producer, Barneby said.

Former sugar exporter Indonesia, with its refinery projects now on stream, had become a useful outlet for Australian sugar, while another former exporter, the Philippines, was likely to become a regular sugar importer, he said.
Barneby saw China as a sugar importer "for several years at least".
Chinese sugar areas had been dislocated by industrialisation in the south, while sugar production may not receive the signals and income to encourage growth, he said.
-- Michael Byrnes Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
